Every Sunday night, millions of people make the same decision. They decide to start something new on Monday. Running, a language, an early bedtime. And on Monday, most of them do not start. I have studied this for fifteen years, and the problem is not laziness. The problem is that deciding feels like progress. When you decide to do something, your brain gives you a small reward, as if the work had already begun. So people stop there. They keep deciding, week after week, and they never actually do anything. What works is almost embarrassingly simple. Do not decide to start running. Put your shoes on. Do not decide to learn a language. Read one page tonight. Make the first step so small that you cannot avoid doing it. The decision is the easy part. The first page is the hard part, and it is the only part that counts.

Learners always ask me the same question. Why do we say I enjoy reading, but I decided to read? Is there a reason, or is it just a list? There is a reason, and it is better than a list. The to form usually points forward. It talks about something that comes after the verb: a plan, a decision, a hope. You decide, and then you read. You agree, and then you send. The ing form usually points at the activity itself, something that is already happening or already known. You enjoy reading while you are reading. You avoid calling because you know what calling is like. The best example is stop. If you stop to buy coffee, you stop walking and you go and buy the coffee. If you stop buying coffee, you never buy it again. Same verb, two directions. Once you hear the direction, most of the list takes care of itself.
